posts.title: The sports bar
posts.description: Look, I get it . The Nazi bar cleaned up its act. A few years, maybe even just a few months ago, it was full of Nazi bullshit and propaganda, and run by a clear Nazi, and that sucked, as it was the only bar in town that showed sports. So you left. Because fuck Nazis and who in their right mind hangs out in a Nazi bar, right? I mean, other than Nazis. But honestly, the other places you tried with your friends showed different sports, or no sports at all. And a lot of the conversations you had were just about how bad the Nazis are, and isn’t this a better place than the old Nazi bar, and thank goodness we’re not Nazis, and hey, fuck those Nazis right? Who needs sports anyway? But then a couple of people mentioned the Nazi bar again, and you got curious. You went along, eventually, because you’ve got to check your assumptions every so often. posts.title: Naming things
posts.description: Hang around a group of engineers for any amount of time, and eventually one will tell you how hard it is to name things. This might seem obvious, even to non-engineers. Good names are tricky. Maybe you think about a good product or brand name, and how hard that is to come by. How many times have you been put off buying something, for example, because it has a bit of a rubbish name? But it’s not a challenge confined to engineers and product designers, or marketing and branding gurus. We all name things, especially now that computers and related devices are such an integral part of our lives. We name folders and files in Google Drive. We name photo albums. We title posts on social media and email subject headings. We give our devices names (whether we know it or not, judging by the number of “[first name]’s iPhone” devices on this coffee shop network). posts.title: Being the room
posts.description: I’ve written before about my computing origin story , and it’s still true. These boxes of sand, they can change the world, but only with the right programming. On its own, a computer isn’t even a fancy calculator. With software, it can be whatever it needs to be. Who wouldn’t want to write software that could change someone’s life for the better? It’s still the dream. I moved into management when I remembered that programming was a means to an end. I had become enamoured with programming as its own craft, but I knew I was never going to be that one programmer that you’d give an impossible problem to, only to have them come back two weeks later with a performant solution and a conference talk ready for you to help them edit. My interests are too varied for that. I realised that I would be better placed to make computers do amazing things as a translator.
